Text: Moving an older patient by pulling on an arm or leg may cause a {{c1::dislocation::musculoskeletal injury}} or a {{c1::fracture::musculoskeletal injury}}.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: pulling an older patient's arm or leg threatens the joint and bone; gripping it threatens the thin skin — tears and bruising.

Why: aging leaves the body less flexible and the bones more brittle, so a pull that a younger patient tolerates can injure an older one.

Pitfall: even without an injury, moving a geriatric patient by the extremities can cause significant pain — and chronic conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis limit movement and add pain of their own.

Text: The skin of a geriatric patient is {{c1::thinner::thicker/thinner}}, leaving it more susceptible to {{c2::tears}} and {{c2::bruising}} when you grip an arm or leg.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: pulling an extremity threatens the joint and bone — dislocation or fracture; gripping threatens the surface — the skin tear.

Pitfall: some older patients cannot lie flat or straighten their arms — extra padding and support may be needed to transport them comfortably.
